<reason>B was the more precise and honest debater in several exchanges, but A built the cleaner path to the motion as written. On reduction, A's state-mandate evidence plus the closing of the interstate relocation valve (which B's own framing acknowledged nationwide coverage removes) survived B's ambiguity attacks, and B never sized the evasion it said would swallow the effect. On harms, B's shortage case narrowed to one admittedly inconclusive anecdote (Alabama) and its discrimination case ended with an admitted absence of causal evidence, leaving the motion's "large increases" threshold unmet; A's motive-shrinking and uniformity arguments stood. B won real micro-exchanges — dissolving A's "contradiction" charge via the compliant/evasive split, exposing the audit-trail blind spot, and noting national simultaneity removes the adjustment source — but these wins raised burdens rather than defeated the proposition, and B's closing was largely recap. A's closing did more decision-framing work, though A's repeated "concession" and "silence" characterizations of B's arguments were overreach that costs rebuttal and grounding credit.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's exposure of the audit-trail blind spot: B's Q2 and R2 showed E-Verify logs only submitted hires, not applicants rejected pre-offer, forcing A to retreat from "detectability" to external enforcement tools (applicant-flow data, paired testing) — a visible, correctly-flagged concession, even though A ultimately survived on the motion's threshold wording.</best_rebuttal>
